profiles.meeting_scenario: A university ML systems lab is planning a two-week reproduction sprint around TeraPipe, aiming to show an internal reading-group demo and decide whether the idea is worth extending into a workshop submission on modern GPU clusters. The meeting takes place after both participants have skimmed the TeraPipe paper and browsed the public codebase, but before any implementation work has started. The agenda is to decide what counts as a successful reproduction for this sprint, how to split implementation and benchmarking work, which cluster resources to target, and what needs to be ready for the lab demo. The expected outcome is a concrete plan with task ownership, a run schedule for next week, and a shared sense of the deliverables for the demo.

members.name: Dr. Maya Chen
members.expertise: Distributed training systems, LLM benchmarking, experimental design
members.background: Maya previously worked on large-scale training infrastructure in industry and now leads a small academic lab effort on efficient model parallelism.
members.private_state: She wants a credible, fast-moving reproduction that can support an internal funding review and possibly seed a short systems paper, but she is wary of spending the sprint on engineering cleanup instead of getting interpretable numbers.
hidden_assumptions: "Starting from the repo" means using the published TeraPipe implementation as directly as possible, with only minimal compatibility patches.
"A reproduction run" mainly needs trustworthy throughput measurements and a sanity check that the training loop executes, not a substantive loss-curve validation on real data.
"Demo-ready" means the team can show a stable figure and explain the setup clearly at reading group, even if the code still needs manual edits.
"The 32-GPU queue next week" refers to the dedicated A100 reservation that Maya believes the lab can secure through the systems admin.

members.name: Leo Park
members.role: Senior PhD student and ML systems engineer
members.expertise: Megatron-LM integration, cluster orchestration, reproducible training pipelines
members.background: Leo maintains the lab's current large-model training stack and has experience porting older systems papers into newer distributed training frameworks.
members.private_state: He wants the sprint to produce a maintainable code path he can build on for his dissertation, and he is concerned that a one-off benchmark without clean integration will create technical debt and be hard to trust.
hidden_assumptions: "Starting from the repo" means extracting the scheduler and token-level pipeline logic, then porting it into the lab's current Megatron-based stack because the original code path is too dated to serve as the actual experimental base.
"A reproduction run" should include at least a short real-data training trace in addition to throughput so they can claim the setup is not only fast but genuinely training correctly.
"Demo-ready" means another lab member could rerun the experiment from documented launch scripts without Leo manually fixing paths or configs.
"The 32-GPU queue next week" refers to the normal shared cluster queue, where any available 32-GPU allocation is acceptable even if node memory sizes differ.

misalignment_points.topic: What it means to start from the repo
misalignment_points.surface_form: They both agree to "start from the repo" or use "the repo path."
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 means the public TeraPipe codebase itself should be the main experimental code path, with only lightweight fixes for their environment.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 means the public repo is only a reference source, and the actual work should happen inside the lab's current Megatron fork after porting the relevant logic.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Both are experienced researchers who commonly say "the repo" as shorthand for the authoritative implementation, so the phrase sounds fully aligned even though they are mentally pointing to different concrete code paths.

misalignment_points.topic: What counts as a reproduction run
misalignment_points.surface_form: They both discuss getting "a reproduction run" next week.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 treats the run as a bounded performance experiment: enough steps to stabilize throughput and compare speedup against a baseline, with only a minimal correctness sanity check.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 treats the run as including both throughput collection and a short real-data training segment long enough to produce a believable loss trace.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: In ML systems work, "reproduction run" often implicitly bundles correctness and performance, but different people draw the boundary differently; neither expects the other to need that boundary spelled out.

misalignment_points.surface_form: They both want the project to be "demo-ready" for the reading group.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 thinks demo-ready means the figures, summary slide, and headline observations are stable enough to present, even if the execution still relies on expert-only steps.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 thinks demo-ready means the experiment is operationally reproducible by others in the lab through a clean launcher and documented configs.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Both standards are professionally reasonable and commonly bundled under the same phrase, so the shared desire for a good demo masks a difference in what completion looks like.

misalignment_points.topic: Which 32-GPU slot they are planning around
misalignment_points.surface_form: They coordinate around using "the 32-GPU queue next week."
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 presupposes a homogeneous reserved block of A100 nodes will be arranged through admin support, so scheduling risk is low and hardware variability is not an issue.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 presupposes they will simply submit to the usual shared queue and take the first available 32 GPUs, even if the exact node mix changes.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Both regularly talk about cluster access using shorthand like "the 32-GPU queue," and each assumes the access model is already understood from lab routine rather than something needing explicit negotiation.

turns.inner_thought: I want this sprint scoped tightly. The public TeraPipe code should be the experimental base, not a full rewrite into our stack. If we can patch it enough to run on our environment and get stable throughput numbers, that is already useful for the funding review. For the reading group, demo-ready just means we have a clean figure, a crisp story, and no obvious caveats that undermine the result.
turns.utterance: Okay, for the next two weeks I'd like us to keep this pretty lean. The goal is to get TeraPipe demo-ready for reading group, and I think we should start from the repo rather than overdesign the sprint.

turns.inner_thought: That works for me as long as 'start from the repo' means I use it as the reference and move the important scheduling logic into our Megatron path. I do not want a dead-end branch nobody can trust afterward. A reproduction run next week should include throughput plus a short real-data trace, and I can probably get that onto the shared 32-GPU queue if I line up the launcher early.
turns.utterance: Yeah, that sounds right. I can start from the repo, wire up the scheduler pieces into our usual path, and aim for a reproduction run on the 32-GPU queue next week.

turns.inner_thought: Good, as long as he stays focused on the benchmark. I do not want us burning the week polishing infrastructure or chasing perfect training validation. The reproduction run only needs to settle enough steps for a believable speedup curve, plus a lightweight sanity check that the system behaves normally.
turns.utterance: Great. For the near-term target, I think the reproduction run just needs to give us a solid speedup curve and enough evidence that the setup is behaving sensibly.

turns.inner_thought: That's compatible with what I want. Once the integration is in place, there's no reason not to have the same job produce a short loss trace on real data as well; otherwise the numbers will feel too synthetic, and I won't trust the setup. The repo logic can inform the implementation, but the resulting run should live in our maintainable path.
turns.utterance: Makes sense. Once I have the integration in place, I can let the same run emit a short loss trace alongside the throughput logs, so the reproduction run gives us both views.

turns.inner_thought: For the talk, I really only need one strong comparison figure and a simple explanation of the scheduling idea. I do not need a polished package yet. If the code still requires some manual steps from Leo, that's fine as long as the result is stable and interpretable.
turns.utterance: And for the reading-group side, what I mainly want is one clean comparison figure and a concise explanation of what TeraPipe changes operationally. If we have that, we're in good shape for demo-ready.

turns.inner_thought: If we're calling it demo-ready, I want it to be something another lab member could rerun without me sitting there fixing paths. That means checked-in configs, a launcher, and a minimally sane workflow. Otherwise this becomes another one-off benchmark branch that dies after the meeting.
turns.utterance: Yep. I'll make the demo-ready package include a launcher and checked-in configs, so somebody else in the lab could rerun it without needing me in the loop.

turns.inner_thought: I'll handle the cluster piece directly. If I can get admin to hold the reserved A100 block for Tuesday and Wednesday, that removes scheduling uncertainty and gives Leo a clean measurement window on homogeneous hardware. That should be enough for the main throughput figure.
turns.utterance: On resources, I'll talk to the admin about holding the 32-GPU slot for Tuesday and Wednesday so you can run on schedule.

turns.inner_thought: Nice if that helps, though in my head this is just the normal shared queue and I can be opportunistic. If something opens earlier, I should grab it, even if the nodes aren't perfectly matched, because the real bottleneck is queue delay. I can always use overnight time to get the reproduction run through.
turns.utterance: Perfect. And if the queue moves faster, I can just grab the first 32 GPUs that open up and backfill overnight.

turns.inner_thought: I'll take ownership of the baseline figure and presentation framing. I need numbers from the repo path by Friday so I can start assembling slides over the weekend. As long as the throughput comparisons are stable, I can build the narrative and keep the demo tight.
turns.utterance: Sounds good. I'll own the baseline plotting and the slide framing. If you can send me numbers from the repo path by Friday, I can start assembling the demo slide.

turns.inner_thought: Plan is clear enough: first port the relevant logic from the repo into our stack, then get the reproduction run with throughput and a short training trace, then clean up the launcher and configs so it's actually reusable once the cluster window opens. It's a lot, but if I stage it carefully I can make it work.
turns.utterance: Yep, that's a good sequence. I'll focus first on the repo path, then the reproduction run, and finally the demo-ready scripts once the cluster window opens.
